title: Second-generation anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies for Alzheimer's disease: current landscape and future perspectives
one_line: A review of second-generation anti-amyloid-beta monoclonal antibodies (aducanumab, lecanemab, donanemab, gantenerumab), their epitopes, trial outcomes, ARIA safety issues, and next-generation delivery strategies.
key_claims: Three second-generation anti-amyloid antibodies have FDA approval — aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab — with lecanemab having received traditional (not just accelerated) approval, which the authors treat as validation of the amyloid cascade hypothesis.

Each antibody targets a distinct Aβ species and epitope: aducanumab plaques (aa 3–7), lecanemab protofibrils (aa 1–16 and 21–29), donanemab N-terminal pyroglutamate Aβ, gantenerumab fibrils (aa 3–11 and 18–27).
Lecanemab's ClarityAD trial showed slowing of cognitive decline and effects on both amyloid-beta and phosphorylated tau levels; aducanumab showed dose-dependent amyloid reduction.
Donanemab's Trailblazer-ALZ trials showed significant amyloid reduction; accelerated approval was initially denied for limited patient data, with later trials more positive.
Gantenerumab gave mixed results — early trials reduced amyloid but the larger Graduate I/II trials showed no significant cognitive improvement, possibly attributable to dosing and delivery.

ARIA (edema ARIA-E, hemorrhage ARIA-H) is the dominant safety liability and is linked to complement cascade and Fc-receptor-mediated signalling; poor blood-brain barrier penetration forces high doses that raise ARIA risk.
limitations: A narrative review, not new experimental or trial data; no head-to-head comparison between antibodies is presented.
Cognitive benefit is described as slowing of decline, not reversal, and amyloid clearance does not consistently translate to clinical benefit (gantenerumab).
Donanemab's evidence base was initially limited by small patient numbers at the time of accelerated approval review.
Blood-brain barrier restriction of antibody entry remains unsolved, constraining the therapeutic window.
Future strategies (ADCs, targeted protein degradation, α Aβ-Gas6 fusion, miRNA and blood-based biomarkers) are proposals or early-stage, not clinically validated.
open_questions: Do combination or personalised biomarker-guided regimens produce clinically meaningful benefit beyond amyloid clearance alone?
Can BBB-crossing formats (ADCs, fusion proteins, degraders) deliver equivalent amyloid clearance at doses that avoid ARIA?
What mechanistic intervention on complement/FcR signalling would decouple ARIA from efficacy?
Would earlier intervention guided by blood-based or microRNA biomarkers change outcomes in pre-symptomatic patients?
Why did gantenerumab fail in Graduate I/II — dosing/delivery, or the fibril epitope itself?
